newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Issing says mark slide is food for thought.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Issing says mark slide is food for thought.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing on Tuesday stressed once again the central bank was worried by the mark's rapid slide and dismissed the idea Germany's economy was too weak to bear an interest rate rise.

In an interview with the magazine Boerse Online, Issing said exchange rates were one of the most important policy guidelines for the Bundesbank after its main indicator, M3 money supply, spelling this out more clearly than in the past.
"The fact that the mark has weakened so fast and so significantly certainly gives us something to think about," he told the magazine in an interview conducted on July 29.
The dollar, which was trading at around 1.8350 marks on July 29, on Tuesday surged to an eight-year high above 1.88 marks, a jump of 22 percent since the start of the year.

But Issing made clear that the dollar's surge would not automatically have immediate policy consequences. "There is no automatic link between the dollar rate and monetary policy decisions," Issing said.

Asked whether the economy could bear an interest rate rise given high unemployment and a stumbling economy, Issing said: "I would disagree with that assessment. We have a clear rise in capacity utilisation and exports are really booming in some areas.

"There are good chances that the government's expected growth rate...of at least 2.5 percent for 1997 will be achieved. The economy is not exactly overheating but it should not be labelled worse than it is," he said.

Issing's comments opened a fresh debate in financial markets already swirling with speculation over whether the Bundesbank could be about to tighten policy, a move which would mark the end of five years of falling German interest rates.

The Bundesbank itself fired markets with the expectation that it could be about to make a long-awaited upward adjustment in interest rates almost two weeks ago -- by deliberately keeping markets guessing about its policy course this summer.

At its final council meeting before a four-week summer break, on July 24, it broke with recent tradition by leaving its options open to readjust its main money market interest rate, the repo, in the middle of the summer break.

On Tuesday, by not setting a repo tender at variable rates alongside its pre-announced fixed rate three percent pact, it defied market expectations that it could pave the way for higher interest rates.
In a variable repo, banks bid for funds at the interest rates of their choice, giving markets greater control.

At the next repo tender on August 12, the central bank would have free rein to set only a variable repo, or a double decker construction of a variable and fixed rate pact, or a fixed tender at either an unchanged rate or a higher level.
But analysts were growing increasingly sceptical that a gentle repo tightening would serve the desired purpose of reining in the mark in the current environment.

Yet they were also sceptical that the Bundesbank could find sufficient domestic justification for a sizeable rate rise. And, they argued, any tightening would be very unpopular with Germany's European neighbours -- particularly France and Italy.

"I would doubt very much that the Bundesbank will make any policy changes in the current environment," said Irgeen Rust, monetary economist at WestLB in Duesseldorf. "They are not going too be panicked into a move."
"Everything now is playing at a psychological level. The situation is not dangerous enough for the central bank to run the risk of making a move which could go badly wrong."
Marius Daheim at Sal Oppenheim agreed. "We think the Bundesbank will stick with a fixed rate repo tender at an unchanged rate," he said. "That view is hinged on the dollar's movements to some extent.

"But a rise of 10 or 20 basis points in the repo would not brake the dollar," he added. "And a markedly higher rate is very unlikely...Any raise at all would not go down well with the European neighbours."
With the Bundesbank facing this dilemma, it could well decide to hold off for a further two weeks, until its full council reconvenes on August 21.

If a significant policy change were deemed necessary, this might well go beyond the confidential policy guidelines given to the Frankfurt-based directorate by the central bank's council on July 24 to govern its decisions through the summer.
